passage:
It was past one in the morning in the hostel common room, and Tanuja was still scrolling. A flood somewhere. A crash on the highway. A thread about how every job would vanish in five years. A video of a fight outside a shopping centre. Each post pulled her to the next.
Zeenat, coming back from the washroom, saw the blue glow. "Still up?"
"Everything is getting worse," Tanuja said, not looking up. "Like, everything. I don't even know why I'm studying."
"What did you actually learn tonight that you didn't know at ten?"
Tanuja opened her mouth, then closed it. Her chest was tight, her tea was cold, and she couldn't name one new fact.
"Phone in my locker till morning?" Zeenat offered. Tanuja hesitated, then handed it over.

qa.q: What time was it in the hostel common room?
qa.a: Past one in the morning.

qa.q: Why does Tanuja feel that everything is getting worse?
qa.a: She has seen bad post after bad post for hours, so the world starts to feel like nothing but floods, crashes and fights, and her worry grows with each one. 😰

qa.q: Which step helped, and what could Tanuja do on other nights?
qa.a: Handing the phone to Zeenat broke the loop; on other nights she could set a time to stop and check news once a day from a calm source.

qa.q: What is it like for Zeenat to find Tanuja scrolling at one in the morning?
qa.a: Zeenat seems worried and wants to help without lecturing, so Zeenat asks a simple question and offers to keep the phone.

grounding: It shows a young adult checking bad news late into the night, growing more distressed while learning nothing new.

passage:
Dear Elizabeth,
Sorry I missed your call on Sunday. I've been in a strange mood. Every night I tell myself I'll read the news for five minutes, and then it's two hours of break-ins, accidents, angry posts and videos of people shouting at each other. Last night I read about three chain-snatchings in our city, and today I didn't want to take the metro to college. I went, of course. Nothing happened. Nobody even looked at me.
It just feels like the world has become so much worse than when we were kids. Everyone online says so. But when I try to say what has actually changed, I can't. I only know I feel worse.
Do you feel this too, over there?
Love,
Salma

qa.q: How many chain-snatchings did Salma read about last night?
qa.a: Three chain-snatchings in their city.

qa.q: Why does Salma feel the world has become so much worse?
qa.a: Salma feels anxious after hours of bad news every night, with everyone online agreeing, so the fear seems like fact even though Salma can't name what has changed.

qa.q: What could Salma try instead of reading for two hours?
qa.a: Set a short, fixed time for news, stop well before bed, and count real days like the calm metro ride as evidence too.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel reading this email?
qa.a: Elizabeth might be worried about Salma's mood and want to gently point out that the metro ride went fine.

grounding: It shows a young adult reading bad news for hours and concluding the world is worse, while fear grows and real information does not.

passage: For the campus radio's Honest Hour, this is Lakshmi. Last semester I got hooked on bad news. It started with one cyclone update. Then I'd wake at 3 a.m. and check: more storms, a bridge collapse, a post saying our generation has no future, a thread about layoffs. Every refresh felt like keeping watch, as if something would sneak up on me if I stopped. My roommate Sangeeta would ask, "Anything new?" and honestly, most nights, no. Same stories, new angry comments. But my heart would be racing and I'd skip breakfast. I told Sangeeta the world was ending. She asked what I'd do differently if it was. I had no answer. I just knew I felt terrible, and scrolling didn't make me know any more.

qa.q: At what time would Lakshmi wake up and check the news?
qa.a: At 3 a.m.

qa.q: Why did scrolling feel like "keeping watch" to Lakshmi?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt anxious that stopping would let something bad sneak up, so each refresh felt like protection and the checking felt necessary even though it brought no new information.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi have done on those 3 a.m. nights?
qa.a: Keep the phone out of reach at night, and if the worry stays heavy, talk to Sangeeta or the college counsellor.

qa.q: What was it like for Sangeeta to share a room with Lakshmi then?
qa.a: Sangeeta likely saw the racing heart and skipped breakfasts and felt worried, asking gentle questions to help Lakshmi notice nothing new was being learned.

grounding: It shows a young adult checking bad news at night, feeling the world is ending while gaining no real information.

passage:
I'm Chandrika. My sister Amandeep, nineteen, came with us to Nani's house in Shimla for the winter break, and I spent most of it watching the top of her head.
She scrolled at breakfast: a fire somewhere, a scam, an angry thread. She scrolled on the walk to the Mall Road and walked into a lamp post. On the second night it snowed for the first time in years. Nani and I were at the window shouting for her. She came, looked for a second, then went back to a video about some crime.
At dinner she said, "Honestly, the world is getting worse every day. It's all falling apart." Nani asked what had actually changed since last week. Amandeep couldn't name anything; she just said, "Everything."
I don't know what she was feeling. She looked tired, and her jaw was tight all week.

qa.q: What did Amandeep walk into on the way to the Mall Road?
qa.a: She walked into a lamp post.

qa.q: How did Amandeep seem to feel during the holiday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Amandeep seemed tired and worried, with her jaw tight all week and saying the world is falling apart, though she could not name anything that had changed.

qa.q: How could Nani's question help Amandeep, and what small step might follow?
qa.a: Asking what had actually changed shows that her fear has grown without new facts; a small step would be to put the phone away for moments like the first snowfall.

qa.q: What was the holiday like for Chandrika?
qa.a: Chandrika spent it watching Amandeep's head bent over the phone, missing shared moments like the snow, and seems worried about Amandeep's tight jaw.

grounding: It shows a young adult checking bad news and negative posts and deciding the world is falling apart, while real information does not change.

passage:
Week 1, Monday: Manjula, twenty, joined a neighbourhood alert group for her area of Mysuru. That night she read about a chain-snatching two streets away and a stray dog chasing a cyclist. She shared both with Shreya. "Did you know it's this bad here?"
Week 2, Friday: She now checked the group before bed, again at two in the morning, and first thing at dawn. Most posts were the same three incidents, reposted and argued over. She stopped her evening walk to the lake and asked Shreya to come with her even to the vegetable shop.
Week 4, Wednesday: Shreya asked, "How many new incidents this month, actually?" Manjula scrolled for a long time. "Two, maybe. But it feels like a hundred." Her hands were cold. She put the phone face down, and five minutes later picked it up again.

qa.q: How many new incidents did Manjula find that month?
qa.a: "Two, maybe."

qa.q: Why does the neighbourhood feel so dangerous to Manjula when she can only find two incidents?
qa.a: Reading the same bad posts again and again, day and night, makes the danger feel constant, so her fear keeps rising even though the real news hardly changes.

qa.q: What turning point came in Week 4, and what could Manjula do with it?
qa.a: Shreya's question showed that "a hundred" was really two; Manjula could set fixed times to check, or leave the group, and slowly go back to her lake walk with Shreya.

qa.q: What is it like for Shreya over these weeks?
qa.a: Shreya goes from getting shocked messages to being needed for trips to the vegetable shop, and seems worried enough to finally ask a careful question.

grounding: It shows a young adult repeatedly checking negative posts and concluding her area is far worse than it is, while distress rises and real information does not.
